title: Rural life comparison; family background
description: Dorothy Anderson compares rural living with urban life, emphasizing community support, friendliness, and convenience. She also introduces personal background details about herself and her husband.

title: Grandparents and parents; childhood memories
description: She discusses her grandparents, her parents' lives in Anaconda, Montana, and her childhood during the Depression era, including family discipline and activities.

title: Education expectations; teaching career
description: She recounts her education, her father's encouragement of college, and her path into teaching, including her early jobs and move to Idaho.

title: Single life in Potlatch; courtship
description: She describes living in teacher housing, social life as a single teacher, meeting her husband, courtship, and early marriage.

title: Childbirth and family planning; relatives nearby
description: She discusses preparation for childbirth, having one child, and the later development of family gatherings when relatives moved closer.

title: Media, reading, and crafts; food preservation
description: She talks about television, magazines, reading habits, needlework and other crafts, and household practices such as gardening, canning, and freezing food.

title: Domestic changes; balancing teaching and family
description: Dorothy Anderson discusses how she stopped canning and preserving fruit as she returned to teaching, explaining the economic and time factors involved. She describes changing meal habits, from three hot meals to lighter salads and sandwiches, and how she arranged childcare for her daughter Sue through Presbyterian kindergarten and grandparents.

title: Teaching career; community organizations
description: Anderson explains her early desire to teach, following her mother and aunts into the profession. She details her involvement in Eastern Star, church women's associations, and homemaker clubs, describing how these organizations connected her to community life in Potlatch.

title: Religion; school as social center
description: Anderson discusses the central role of Presbyterian church activities and her daughter Sue's extensive school involvement in band, sports, and National Honor Society. She describes how school functions served as the family's primary social activity and entertainment.

title: Educational changes; student discipline
description: Anderson observes changes in children's behavior and responsibility levels, noting that rural students have more 4-H and animal care duties than town children. She discusses evolving dress codes and student attitudes toward authority.

title: Family life; leisure activities
description: Anderson shares details about her daughter's education at University of Idaho and St. Martin's College, and describes family vacations to the Oregon coast and California. She explains how they adjusted their farming operation to prioritize travel time together.

title: Domestic technology; changing roles
description: Anderson compares modern conveniences and appliances to her mother's era, recalling the icebox and horse-drawn ice wagons of her childhood. She discusses her evolving role in meal preparation, her husband's supportive attitude toward her working, and their partnership in household decisions.

title: Women's employment; rural challenges
description: Anderson reflects on changing attitudes toward women working outside the home, sharing her daughter's experience as a working wife. She discusses the economic and personal fulfillment women's employment provides, contrasting it with traditional homemaking roles.

title: Small town life; social adjustment
description: Anderson offers advice for newcomers to rural communities, suggesting they must actively seek involvement in organizations. She describes her daughter's perspective on limited social options in small towns versus larger cities.

title: Fulfilling experiences; home life
description: Anderson lists her happiest moments, including her daughter's success, her husband joining church activities, earning her master's degree, and building their home together. She reflects on her husband's craftsmanship and their collaborative domestic life.

title: Rural education; drug awareness
description: Anderson explains her preference for rural schools, noting she feels safe around students and knows their family backgrounds. She mentions the community's experience with drugs while emphasizing the advantage of small class sizes and personal knowledge of students.

title: Moscow Mountain; local geography
description: Anderson briefly discusses Moscow Mountain as a recreational area, though she has not visited for picnics. She touches on school district boundaries and where children from that area attend school.

title: Women's initiatives; school demographics
description: Anderson discusses more women returning to work after having children, sharing one former student's experience. She describes declining school enrollment, changing class sizes, and the effectiveness of special education programs.

title: Country-versus-town distinctions; conclusion
description: Anderson contrasts past and present differences between farm and town children, noting rural kids once wore overalls and faced teasing but now often have more responsibilities. She discusses reading problems, special education, and how consolidation changed student interactions.
